newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends firm in US after steady Fed, Dow jump.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends firm in US after steady Fed, Dow jump.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed against the yen in U.S. dealings on Tuesday, but keyed off a resurgent stock market for the second day in a row to close higher versus the mark.
The Dow Jones industrial average slipped from early afternoon highs after the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announced, as expected, that there would be no change in U.S. interest rates.
But it clawed its way back in late trading, ending up 115 points at 7,918 after rising 109 points on Monday.

Dealers said that Tuesday's stock gains, taken together with Monday's advance, helped reassure nervous dollar bulls that last Friday's mammoth 247 point retreat in the Dow was not the beginning of large and lengthy downturn in stocks.
"As long as the stock market remains positive the dollar should remain well bid," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
The dollar ended the day at 1.8400/10 marks, up from 1.8347/52 at the open. It closed at 118.25/35 yen, virtually unchanged from its opening rate of 118.29/34.
Propping dollar/mark throughout the U.S. session was the Bundesbank's decision on Tuesday to stick with its fixed rate repo at 3.0 percent.
Although fears the Bundesbank could switch to a variable rate repo had diminished over the past week, dealers said the news proved dollar-supportive.

The Bundesbank also cooled talk that it might push up interest rates at an upcoming policy meeting on Thursday by announcing a sharp slowdown in M3 money supply growth -- an indicator the central bank uses to gauge future inflation.

"The Bundesbank kept its repo at a fixed rate and that took any potential for dollar selling out of the market right there," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
Dollar gains against the yen were capped by mark/yen sales and nervousness ahead of U.S. trade figures for June, due to be released on Wednesday.

The total U.S. trade deficit, which stood at $10.23 billion in May, is expected to edge up slightly to $10.36 billion in June. Traders said a large increase in the bilateral gap with Japan could fuel buying of yen for dollars.
Nevertheless, dealers remained bullish on the dollar's prospects, with some predicting a decoupling from volatile asset markets in the coming days.
"Our inclination is still that the bond and equity markets will calm down and the dollar uptrend will resume," said Ricardo Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.
"Our game plan has been to buy dollars on dips," he added, noting that he expected dollar/mark to encounter some resistance at the 1.8480 level.
In other trade on Tuesday, the dollar pushed up to 1.5142/52 Swiss francs from 1.5115/20 at the open, and rose to Canadian $1.3941/46 from an opening rate of C$1.3895/00.
The British pound ended flat at $1.6060/70 and the Australian dollar advanced to $0.7420/25 from $0.7386/91 at the outset of trading.
